item.title: Bank of America’s Hartnett says buy tech bonds as relative returns hit 30-year low
item.description:
Hartnett’s call puts tech credit in contrast with tech equities. Bond investors are being paid more to fund the AI build-out, while shareholders are losing the buyback support that underpinned megacap returns for years. Wider default swap spreads across the biggest names show credit markets are still pricing AI as a distinct risk, although Oracle’s retreat from its October peak hints at some stabilisation. For equities, the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF closing Friday just below Hartnett’s $70 threshold is an early warning on his year-end rally framework. With long-dated Treasury yields still elevated and central banks tightening, the rate backdrop remains the main obstacle to a broader recovery in risk appetite.

-

After a year of being flooded with AI debt, tech bonds now look like the better-protected way into the boom, Hartnett argues, because the hyperscalers have started treating creditors better than shareholders.

Summary:

  • Bank of America’s Michael Hartnett recommends buying US tech bonds, which have fallen about 9% in 2026, leaving their returns relative to investment grade at a 30-year low
  • Heavy supply is the main driver, with AI hyperscalers issuing $182 billion of bonds this year against $17 billion in 2024, pushing long-dated megacap yields to between 6% and 8%
  • Hartnett says hyperscalers’ $89 billion of equity issuance and a collapse in buybacks to an annualised $14 billion favour bondholders
  • S&P Global Market Intelligence data show five-year credit default swap spreads have widened sharply across Big Tech since September, though Oracle’s has eased from its October peak
  • Hartnett expects relief in the first half of 2027 and says a year-end rally needs the Magnificent Seven ETF to hold $70, a level it slipped just below on Friday

Bank of America chief investment strategist Michael Hartnett is recommending investors buy technology bonds, arguing that a borrowing binge by AI hyperscalers has pushed tech debt to levels that offer value after a punishing year.

In his latest "Flow Show" note, Hartnett said US technology bonds have fallen about 9% in 2026, leaving their total return relative to the broader investment-grade index at a 30-year low. The main cause has been supply. Hyperscalers have issued $182 billion of bonds this year to fund data centres, up from $17 billion in 2024, and investors have demanded higher yields to absorb it. Long-dated bonds from the Magnificent Seven and other AI leaders now yield between 6% and 8%, levels Hartnett considers attractive, while CoreWeave’s 2031 high-yield bond yields more than 14%.

Hartnett argues the balance of power is shifting toward creditors. He pointed to Meta’s recent share sale as a sign the company is giving bondholders more consideration, since raising equity rather than adding debt strengthens the balance sheet behind its bonds. Hyperscalers have raised $89 billion through equity issuance this year, while buybacks have dropped to an annualised $14 billion from $105 billion in 2024. Hartnett said the era of large buybacks is over and that retaining cash benefits bondholders. He also expects AI bonds’ long run of underperformance against AI stocks to end.

The spending pressure is considerable. Bank of America projects AI capital expenditure rising to $1.2 trillion in 2027 from $240 billion in 2024, while free cash flow swings from $240 billion to a negative $180 billion over the same period. Hartnett said bond markets are now imposing discipline on the AI expansion.

Credit markets have been signalling stress. S&P Global Market Intelligence data as of Friday showed five-year credit default swap spreads widening sharply across major tech companies since early September, with Oracle’s rising to 276 basis points from 210 and Nvidia’s to 129 from 84. Oracle’s spread has, however, eased from an October 20 peak of 325, an early sign of stabilisation. S&P Global said in October that investors increasingly treat AI exposure as a separate credit risk.

Hartnett expects investors to stay risk-averse until the global rate-hiking cycle ends, noting central banks have raised rates 42 times in the past six months. He sees relief in the first half of 2027 from geopolitical peace, sharply lower oil prices and an end to hikes. In the meantime, he said a year-end rally depends on the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF holding $70 and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF holding $520. The Magnificent Seven fund closed just below its threshold on Friday, while the semiconductor fund remains about 8% above its level.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BTCPay Server tells operators to shut down after reports of hot wallets being drained
item.description:
BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers.

---

Adding to concerens re the drain last week:

  • investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Binance hack shakes crypto

---

In a post on X, the project asked anyone running an instance to take it offline with its shutdown command until the investigation is complete. BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken.

A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds. That convenience makes it a bigger target than offline storage. The incident involves software built around Bitcoin, not the Bitcoin network itself.

The warning follows two recent security events at the project. On October 29, BTCPay released emergency version 2.4.7 to fix one critical and several medium-risk vulnerabilities. In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation. At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected.

That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw. BTCPay has not said whether the new attacks are linked to the vulnerabilities fixed last week.

What to watch next

The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected. Loss figures and reports from named merchants will show the scale of the problem. In August, BTCPay narrowed the scope considerably after its first alert, so the initial warning may not reflect the final picture. Until the project gives an all-clear, operators holding funds in a BTCPay hot wallet should follow its shutdown advice.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US clocks fall back: Wall Street opens an hour later for traders in Asia and Europe
item.description:
The change doesn’t alter exchange hours, but it does shift when global liquidity overlaps. Asia-Pacific desks now see US cash trading start and finish an hour later on their clocks, which narrows the gap between the Wall Street close and the Asian open and changes when US-driven moves first reach Asian markets. For Europe, the London and New York overlap returns to its normal winter shape after a week in which the US was an hour closer than usual. The main operational risk is mis-timed orders, alerts and automated strategies set to local clocks, particularly around US data releases and the Sunday futures reopen.

---

The exchanges haven’t moved an inch, but for anyone trading New York from Sydney, Tokyo or London, Wall Street just pushed its alarm clock back an hour.

Summary:

  • The US and most of eastern Canada moved clocks back one hour on Sunday, November 1, ending daylight saving time
  • Exchange hours are unchanged in local time, so the impact falls on traders outside North America
  • The New York cash equity session, 0930 to 1600 US Eastern, now runs from 1430 to 2100 GMT, an hour later than before
  • US economic data at 0830 ET now lands at 1330 GMT, and Fed decisions at 1400 ET at 1900 GMT
  • With Australia on daylight time since October 4, Sydney is now 16 hours ahead of New York, the widest gap of the year

Traders outside North America need to adjust their schedules this week after the US and most of eastern Canada moved their clocks back one hour on Sunday, November 1, ending daylight saving time for the year.

Exchange hours have not changed in local terms. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq still open at 0930 US Eastern and close at 1600 ET, and the Toronto Stock Exchange keeps the same hours. Because New York is now on Eastern Standard Time, five hours behind GMT, the cash session now runs from 1430 to 2100 GMT, an hour later than it did last week for anyone watching from London, Asia or Australia.

The shift carries through to the economic calendar. Most US data released at 0830 ET, including payrolls and inflation figures, now arrive at 1330 GMT, while Federal Reserve decisions at 1400 ET now land at 1900 GMT. CME Globex futures, which reopen at 1800 ET on Sunday and pause daily from 1700 to 1800 ET, now restart at 2300 GMT. The 1700 ET New York close that marks the turn of the FX trading day now falls at 2200 GMT.

The effect is largest for traders in the Asia-Pacific region. Australia’s eastern states moved to daylight saving on October 4, so Sydney and Melbourne are now 16 hours ahead of New York, the widest gap of the year. The US cash open now comes at 0130 Sydney time (ain't that just peachy ...) and close at 0800, while the weekly futures reopen arrives at 1000 on Monday morning. In Tokyo, which does not observe daylight saving, Wall Street now trades from 2330 to 0600, and in Singapore and Hong Kong from 2230 to 0500.

European traders already went through their own change. Most of Europe ended summer time on October 25, leaving a one-week window in which New York opened at 1330 in London. That window has now closed, and the London and New York overlap is back to its usual winter pattern.

There is also a new wrinkle in Canada. British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories did not move their clocks back this year after ending seasonal time changes, so some Canadian cities are now an hour out of step with their US neighbours. That has no effect on the Toronto and Montreal exchanges, as Ontario and Quebec followed the US change.

The next shift comes on March 14, 2027, when US clocks move forward again.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI - Ukrainian drones hit three Russian refineries in 72 hours, ending US-sought pause
item.description:
The renewed campaign puts Russian refined product supply back in focus, particularly diesel, at a time when the Iran war has already tightened global energy markets. Damage to processing units, including a diesel hydrotreater at Novokuybyshevsk, could curb Russian fuel exports and support refining margins if outages last, although the extent of damage has not been independently verified. Russia may also redirect more unrefined crude to export if domestic processing is disrupted. The political angle adds uncertainty: Washington has pressed Kyiv to stop these strikes and has blamed them for high fuel prices, so any US response after Tuesday’s midterms could shift the outlook for Russian energy flows and sanctions.

---

Earlier:

  • OPEC+ holds December targets steady for third month as Hormuz disruption persists
  • Iran says two tankers hit mines in Hormuz as Tehran offers two-day reopening plan

---

Kyiv’s informal energy truce with Washington has ended in smoke over three Russian refineries, with Ukraine betting that hitting Moscow’s oil revenue is worth the diplomatic cost days before the US midterms.

Summary:

  • Ukrainian drones reportedly struck three Russian refineries over three consecutive nights from October 30, ending a pause of about two weeks in such attacks
  • The targets were Rosneft’s Novokuybyshevsk refinery in Samara, the Bashneft-Novoil plant in Ufa and LUKOIL’s NORSI refinery in Kstovo, with combined capacity of about 33 million tonnes a year, roughly 10% of Russia’s total
  • The pause followed repeated US demands to halt refinery strikes, which Trump has blamed for high global fuel prices; the Kremlin said Kyiv was now ignoring US wishes
  • Kyiv has not formally acknowledged the refinery attacks and said it was responding to intensifying Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure
  • Trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are expected later this month

Ukraine has resumed drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, hitting three major plants over three consecutive nights and ending a pause of about two weeks that came amid heavy pressure from the Trump administration to stop such strikes.

The first strike, overnight on October 30, set fire to Rosneft’s Novokuybyshevsk refinery in the Samara region. That was followed by an attack on an industrial area of Ufa, home to the Bashneft-Novoil refinery, and then by a strike overnight on November 1 on LUKOIL’s NORSI refinery in Kstovo, one of Russia’s largest, according to Ukrainian monitoring group Dnipro Osint and Russian state media. Together the three plants can process about 33 million tonnes of crude a year, roughly 10% of Russia’s refining capacity, though that figure reflects capacity targeted rather than confirmed output losses. Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said it was involved in the Novokuybyshevsk and Kstovo strikes, including hits on a diesel hydrotreating unit.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Ukraine had not struck a Russian refinery since October 15, or any Russian oil infrastructure since October 20, as US officials repeatedly pressed Kyiv to stop. Trump has blamed the attacks for high global fuel prices, which energy experts mostly attribute to the US-Iran war, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel. European allies had reportedly urged Kyiv to wait until after Tuesday’s US midterm elections.

Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent they never agreed to a US request for a 30-day pause. The Kremlin said Kyiv was now simply ignoring Washington’s wishes.

President Volodymyr Zelensky has not acknowledged the refinery strikes, in what appears to be an effort to avoid antagonising Washington. He has said Ukraine is obliged to respond to Russia’s intensifying campaign against its energy system. Russian drones and missiles killed at least 27 civilians across Ukraine on Thursday, and overnight strikes on Sunday cut power to hundreds of thousands of households, with Kyiv facing outages of up to 10 hours. Zelensky has said Ukraine wants stronger protection for its own energy infrastructure in return for halting refinery attacks.

Diplomacy continues alongside the escalation. Trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are expected later this month, and the Kremlin said President Vladimir Putin was willing to speak directly to Zelensky by phone. Russia’s core territorial demands, however, remain unchanged, which limits the prospects for a broader breakthrough. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia’s AI investment ambitions hit by another data centre setback
item.description:
The delay adds to a run of setbacks that point to rising execution risk across Australia’s (and global) data centre sector, where permitting, energy supply and community opposition are all lengthening timelines. Listed developers and landlords such as NextDC and Goodman have already pulled back or delayed projects this year, and a regulatory hold on a project in one of the country’s most sparsely populated regions suggests location alone will not clear the path. Slower approvals push out revenue for developers and could weigh on valuations that assume fast AI-driven growth. The setback is also a potential headwind for Northern Territory gas developers, whose demand outlook increasingly relies on data centre power.

- Even a cattle station almost 700 km from the nearest city is not remote enough to escape regulatory delay, as Australia’s data centre pipeline runs into planning, power and social-licence hurdles. And populist clap-trap too. 

Summary:

  • Startup Energy North has dropped the June 2028 first power date for its planned 1 GW gas and solar data centre in the Northern Territory
  • The territory’s environment regulator suspended its seven-week deadline to set assessment terms, citing the need to consult the federal government, which is still developing data centre policy
  • The regulator flagged 10 potential impacts, including strain on water systems and disruption to Aboriginal sacred sites, and said it had little confidence in the proposed mitigation measures
  • Energy North says it remains committed and will confirm timing once environmental impact statement terms are set
  • The delay follows NextDC’s postponement of a Melbourne expansion over energy supply and Goodman’s withdrawal of a Sydney project amid resident opposition

The developer of one of Australia’s largest planned data centres has abandoned its target start date after the Northern Territory’s environment regulator said it needed more time to set the project’s environmental requirements, Reuters reported in an exclusive on Sunday.

Startup Energy North had given a first power date of June 2028 for Project Ares, a 1 gigawatt gas and solar-powered data centre planned for a cattle station almost 700 km from the nearest city. In an October 7 ruling, the territory’s Environment Protection Authority suspended its seven-week deadline for deciding which hurdles the project must clear. It said it would seek advice from the federal government, which is still developing policy expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure, and gave no new timeframe.

Energy North told Reuters the 2028 date had been indicative and that it was no longer working to it. The company said it would confirm timing once the regulator set out terms for an environmental impact statement. It declined to identify its financiers.

The regulator’s ruling on the roughly 190 sq km campus, which would include gas turbines, a solar farm, an airstrip and housing for 4,300 construction workers, identified 10 potential impacts, ranging from strain on water systems to disruption of Aboriginal sacred sites. It also said it had low confidence that the proposed measures would manage significant impacts effectively.

The delay is the largest timing setback for an Australian data centre so far. It follows NextDC’s decision this month to delay a Melbourne expansion over energy supply concerns, and Goodman’s withdrawal of a Sydney project after resident opposition. One urban planner told Reuters that planning frameworks were not designed for proposals of this kind, and that community concern was increasingly affecting real projects.

The setback undercuts the Northern Territory’s pitch that its vast, sparsely populated land and abundant sunshine make it a faster route for AI investment than Australia’s cities. With the territory government reportedly in talks with 12 data centre-related projects, approval risk is becoming a central question for the sector’s growth plans. 

No data centre for you!

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia’s factory PMI stuck at 49.6 as new orders drop at fastest pace since 2024
item.description:
The survey has an uncomfortable mix for policymakers: demand and output are contracting, but input costs and selling prices are rising faster. Firms cited higher interest rates among the reasons for weaker orders, while the pricing data suggest inflation pressure in the goods sector is building rather than fading, which complicates any case for policy relief. The Middle East war is feeding directly into Australian factory costs through fuel, freight and delivery delays, so further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz poses an upside risk to goods inflation. For the Australian dollar, the release adds to signs of softer domestic activity without offering a clear disinflation signal.

---

RBA expected to raise its cash rate on Tuesday, November 3, 2026:

  • RBA set for back-to-back hike after hot CPI, says Natixis’ Garcia Herrero

---

Australian factories are being squeezed from both sides, with orders shrinking at the fastest pace in nearly two years while war-related shipping delays push costs and prices higher.

Summary:

  • The S&P Global Australia Manufacturing PMI held at 49.6 in October, a second month below 50 and the joint-lowest since December 2024
  • New orders fell at the steepest rate in almost two years, which firms blamed on rising prices, higher interest rates and weaker demand; export orders fell only marginally
  • Employment fell for a second month, at the fastest pace in seven months, and purchasing and inventories were cut
  • Delivery times lengthened at one of the sharpest rates since mid-2022, partly due to shipment delays linked to the Middle East war and port congestion
  • Input costs rose at the fastest pace since June, and selling prices rose more quickly for the first time in five months, at an above-average rate
  • Business confidence improved from September’s low but stayed below its long-run average

Australia’s manufacturing sector contracted for a second straight month in October, as the sharpest drop in new orders in almost two years coincided with worsening supply conditions and rising costs, according to S&P Global survey data released on Sunday at 2200 GMT (1700 US Eastern).

The S&P Global Australia Manufacturing PMI was unchanged at 49.6, below the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction and level with its lowest reading since December 2024. Output fell at the same solid pace as in September, which S&P Global described as one of the steepest declines since late 2024.

Demand was the main weakness. New orders fell at the fastest rate since December 2024, and survey respondents cited rising prices, higher interest rates and a deterioration in underlying demand. Export orders fell for a second month, though only marginally. Manufacturers responded by cutting staff at the fastest pace in seven months, reducing purchasing and running down both input and finished goods inventories. Backlogs of work fell more quickly as spare capacity increased.

Supply conditions also deteriorated. Suppliers’ delivery times lengthened at one of the sharpest rates since mid-2022, with firms pointing to shipment delays linked in part to the Middle East war, as well as port congestion. Those delays added to shipping costs, contributing to the fastest rise in input prices since June, alongside higher raw material, supplier and fuel costs.

Manufacturers passed some of that pressure on to customers. Selling prices rose at a faster pace for the first time in five months, at a rate above the series average.

An economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence described the start of the fourth quarter as a double hit for Australian manufacturers, with supply constraints adding to deteriorating demand.

There was a modest bright spot in sentiment. Firms remained positive about output over the next 12 months, and confidence recovered somewhat from September’s low, though it remained below its long-run average. Whether that improvement holds is likely to depend on how quickly shipping disruption eases and whether demand stabilises as borrowing costs and prices weigh on customers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says US and Canada have ‘concept’ of a deal, two days before midterms
item.description:
Taken at face value, a thaw in US-Canada trade relations would support the Canadian dollar and trade-exposed Canadian equities, which have carried the cost of months of tit-for-tat tariffs. Markets are likely to discount the headline until there is text to read, though, because neither side has said what tariffs would change or when. The timing, two days before midterms in which tariffs on Canada are a live issue in some border states, also invites scepticism over how much is policy and how much is campaign messaging. Any detail from the negotiating teams in the coming weeks will matter far more to the loonie than Sunday’s remarks.

--

Washington and Ottawa are now very close to a deal in concept, which is reassuring for anyone who trades concepts, while everyone else waits for something with tariff rates in it.

Summary:

  • Trump said on Sunday that the US and Canada have the concept of a very good trade deal and are very close to an agreement, but gave no details
  • He said he spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday and that the deal would be good for US farmers
  • Carney described a good conversation that built on recent constructive talks about the outlines of a mutually beneficial deal
  • Carney said any deal must create jobs, improve affordability and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty, with teams working toward it over the coming weeks
  • The two countries have imposed billions of dollars in tariffs on each other, an issue in some US border states ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Washington and Ottawa have the “concept” of a new trade deal and are very close to an agreement, though he declined to say what it might contain.

Speaking to reporters after arriving in Dubuque, Iowa, Trump said he had spoken with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday. He described the deal under discussion as very good, and said it would benefit American farmers and the country as a whole. He did not give a timeline or any detail on tariffs, market access or which sectors would be covered.

A concept is, of course, a well-established stage in trade diplomacy. It sits somewhere after a phone call and some distance before anything a customs officer could use. For now, markets and exporters on both sides of the border have an adjective, “very good”, rather than a document.

Carney offered a similarly upbeat, if slightly more measured, account. In a post on X, he said he had a good conversation with Trump about the future of trade between the two countries. He said the exchange built on recent constructive discussions about the outlines of a mutually beneficial deal. Carney said such an agreement should create jobs, improve affordability and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty, adding that negotiating teams would work over the coming weeks to deliver it. His description puts the two leaders roughly in agreement, with a concept on one side and outlines on the other.

The comments follow months of trade conflict, with both countries imposing billions of dollars in tariffs on each other. The dispute has become a political issue in some northern US border states, including Michigan and Maine, ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The next test is whether the coming weeks of talks produce concrete terms. Until negotiators set out which tariffs would be removed or reduced, and on what schedule, the deal remains more aspiration than agreement. Businesses on both sides of the border will be looking for something they can price. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Monday, November 2, 2026 - another China PMI
item.description:
China’s private-sector manufacturing PMI is due at 01:45 GMT on Monday (20:45 US Eastern on Sunday), with economists expecting factory activity to keep growing in October, though at a slower pace than in September.

The RatingDog China General Manufacturing PMI, compiled by S&P Global, is forecast to ease to 51.6 from 52.1, according to a Reuters poll. That would still leave the index comfortably above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction. September’s reading beat expectations and was the strongest in five months, supported by firmer demand at home and abroad, with foreign sales growing at their fastest pace in seven months.

The release follows a weak set of official figures on Saturday. The National Bureau of Statistics manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 from 50.1, well below the 50.0 expected in the same Reuters poll, and new export orders dropped to 48.7. Statisticians attributed much of the decline to seasonal factors, including a pullback in overseas orders after a strong September.

The two surveys often diverge. The RatingDog index samples a smaller group of around 650 firms with a heavier tilt toward export-oriented manufacturers, and it collects responses in the second half of each month. The official survey covers more than 3,000 companies at month-end. The private gauge has typically produced the brighter of the two readings, and that gap was clear in September.

Even so, Saturday’s slide in official export orders raises the risk that the RatingDog reading also comes in below forecast, given its exporter focus. A print close to consensus would suggest the official weakness was largely seasonal. A sharp miss would add to concerns about China’s fourth-quarter momentum and to pressure for more policy support, as Chinese stocks come off their worst month in more than a decade.

The data are likely to be watched closely by traders in the yuan, the Australian dollar and industrial metals.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s central bank, regulators to meet on stock support after record 12-week slide
item.description:
Monday’s session in mainland China and Hong Kong is the first chance for equities to react to the reports, and the prospect of state-backed support may help sentiment at the open after October’s heavy selling. Whether that lasts is likely to depend on detail. Traders have already seen last month’s measures fail to halt the slide, so the scale and terms of any expanded relending facility will matter more than the signal alone. A credible support package could also ease some pressure on the yuan and on broader Asian risk appetite. Without concrete steps, the combination of contracting PMIs and doubts over AI earnings leaves the downside case in place.

---

After a record losing streak in Chinese stocks, Beijing appears to be reaching for more support tools, though last month showed that a signal on its own is not enough. Info via Bloomberg (gated). 

Summary:

  • The People’s Bank of China will meet the financial and securities regulators and major banks on Monday to discuss market support tools, Chinese media reported
  • The talks are expected to focus on improving a relending programme that funds share buybacks and stake increases
  • Some securities firms and funds have received notice of the meeting, and industry participants see it as groundwork for further stabilisation steps
  • The CSI 300 fell 8.5% in October into a bear market, a record 12th straight weekly decline and the worst month in more than a decade
  • Measures announced last month have not stemmed losses, amid a weak economy, doubts over AI earnings, and October PMIs back in contraction

China’s central bank is set to meet the country’s financial regulators and major banks on Monday to discuss tools aimed at supporting the stock market, according to Chinese media reports, as authorities face mounting pressure to halt a steep slide in equities.

The People’s Bank of China will hold talks with the National Financial Regulatory Administration, the China Securities Regulatory Commission and leading banks to study how to improve a relending programme for share buybacks and stake increases, financial news outlet Cailian reported on Sunday, citing people in the industry. The scheme lets companies and major shareholders draw on bank lending, backed by central bank funding, to buy their own shares.

The 21st Century Business Herald reported that some securities firms and funds had been notified of the meeting. The newspaper said people in the industry were speculating that the talks were likely preparation by regulators for further action to stabilise the market. There has been no official confirmation of the meeting’s agenda or any planned measures.

A new state-backed push would add to steps taken last month to steady the equity market. Those efforts have so far failed to turn sentiment, as a weak domestic economy and doubts over earnings from artificial intelligence weigh on investors. The CSI 300 index of major Shanghai and Shenzhen stocks fell 8.5% in October, entering a bear market. It was a record 12th straight week of declines and the worst month for Chinese stocks in more than a decade.

The sell-off has coincided with new signs of economic strain. Official purchasing managers’ indexes released on Saturday showed manufacturing and non-manufacturing activity both slipped back into contraction in October, with the factory gauge falling to 49.3 and the non-manufacturing index to 49.7.

The outcome of Monday’s meeting will be watched closely for signs of the scale and speed of any new support. A meaningful expansion of the relending programme would signal that Beijing is prepared to put more firepower behind the market. A meeting that produces only incremental tweaks risks repeating last month’s experience, when policy steps did not reverse the downturn. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: OPEC+ holds December targets steady for third month as Hormuz disruption persists
item.description:
The rollover was widely expected and does little to change near-term supply, because most of the producers involved cannot reach their existing targets while Hormuz flows remain disrupted. That leaves physical availability tied to the waterway rather than to OPEC+ policy, a point reinforced by Iran’s claim on Sunday that two tankers hit mines and exploded there. For oil traders, the near-term risk is still skewed toward supply disruption. The medium-term counterweight is the surplus forecasters see if Gulf barrels return in 2027, which puts the November 29 quota decision at the centre of next year’s supply outlook.

---

OPEC+ chose to wait rather than act, keeping December targets flat because the Iran war, not quota policy, is setting how much Gulf oil actually reaches the market.

Summary:

  • Seven core OPEC+ producers led by Saudi Arabia kept December production targets unchanged at an online meeting on Sunday, with no further adjustments announced
  • It is the third straight month of steady targets, after the group finished unwinding 1.65 million bpd of 2023 voluntary cuts in September
  • About 2 million bpd of cuts agreed in 2022 remain in place until the end of 2026
  • Gulf members are boosting exports disrupted by the Iran war, but most are still producing below target
  • A capacity review is under way to set 2027 baselines, and the full 21-member group meets on November 29
  • The decision came as Iran said two tankers struck mines and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz

Seven core OPEC+ producers agreed on Sunday to keep their oil production targets for December unchanged, confirming expectations that further policy changes will wait until next year as the Iran war continues to disrupt Gulf exports. Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman made the decision at a videoconference, according to a statement from OPEC, which announced no additional adjustments.

The decision extends a pause that began after the group completed the phased unwinding of 1.65 million barrels per day of voluntary cuts in September. Targets were then held flat for October and November. A further layer of about 2 million bpd of cuts, covering most members, remains in force until the end of 2026. The seven also reaffirmed their commitment to full conformity with the Declaration of Cooperation, the agreement that underpins the wider alliance, and said they would keep meeting monthly.

The practical effect of the targets is limited for now. Gulf producers have been raising exports that have been disrupted for months by the conflict, but most are still pumping well below their quotas because of restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. That disruption was underlined on Sunday, when Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers struck mines and exploded while transiting the strait without Iranian authorisation, a claim that has not been independently verified.

Attention now turns to November 29, when all 21 members of OPEC+ are due to meet and analysts expect the group to set its 2027 production framework. One analyst described Sunday’s decision as the easy one, warning that the group faces a very difficult call on next year. Planning is complicated by uncertainty over the course of the war, how quickly traffic through Hormuz recovers, and how large a surplus could emerge once disrupted barrels return.

Before setting those quotas, the group needs to finish a review of members’ production capacity during the fourth quarter. People familiar with the process say this will determine the baselines for future quotas and shape plans to unwind the remaining cuts. The war has disrupted capacity expansion projects across the Middle East, which has made estimates of future output potential more uncertain. The International Energy Agency and other forecasters have warned that supply could exceed demand in 2027 if Gulf flows return to normal, raising the stakes for the decision at the end of this month.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s factory and services PMI gauges both drop below 50 as fourth quarter starts on a weak note
item.description:
Because the data came out on a Saturday, Monday’s Asian session is the first chance for markets to price the miss. Softer Chinese factory demand is usually a headwind for industrial metals such as copper and iron ore, and for China-sensitive currencies including the yuan and the Australian dollar. Chinese equities may be partly cushioned by expectations of more policy support. For oil, a weaker demand signal from a key crude buyer would normally weigh on prices, but for now it is likely to be overshadowed by supply risk in the Strait of Hormuz. Price sub-indices that are easing but still elevated also weaken the case for reading the release as disinflationary.

---

Earlier

  • ICYMI: Morgan Stanley sees 10%-15% more downside for Chinese offshore stocks before a bottom

---

China’s brief return to factory growth lasted a month, with October’s PMIs slipping below 50 across the board and putting Beijing’s stimulus intentions back in the spotlight.

Summary:

  • China’s official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 in October from 50.1, below the 49.9 median forecast and back under the 50 line separating expansion from contraction
  • Production fell to 49.8, new orders to 49.4 and new export orders to 48.7; large firms held at 50.2, while medium and small firms came in at 48.4 and 47.5
  • The non-manufacturing PMI dropped to 49.7 from 50.2, and the composite output index fell to 49.7 from 50.7, with finance the only major service category in decline
  • The NBS cited seasonal factors, including a pullback in export orders after September’s surge, softer post-holiday consumer demand and demand pulled forward before National Day
  • Input prices eased to 56.8 and output prices to 51.7, both still above year-earlier levels
  • Beijing is targeting 4.5% to 5% growth this year and has signalled it is ready to add stimulus if conditions worsen

China’s manufacturing sector slipped back into contraction in October. The official purchasing managers’ index fell to 49.3 from 50.1 in September, according to data released on Saturday by the National Bureau of Statistics and the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. The reading fell short of the 49.9 median forecast in a Bloomberg survey of economists and dropped below the 50 threshold that separates expansion from contraction, reversing September’s return to growth.

The weakness on the factory side was broad. The production sub-index fell 1.9 points to 49.8 and new orders fell 1.1 points to 49.4, while new export orders dropped to 48.7, leaving all three below 50 in the same month. Large manufacturers stayed just in expansion at 50.2, but medium and small firms recorded 48.4 and 47.5 respectively. High-technology and equipment manufacturing bucked the trend, with readings of 51.3 and 50.6.

Activity outside manufacturing also softened. The non-manufacturing PMI, which covers services and construction, fell to 49.7 from 50.2, and the composite output index dropped a full point to 49.7. The NBS said finance was the only major service category to record a decline in business activity, and that its drop was relatively sharp. Water transport, postal services, and internet and software services all held above 55. Construction activity was also weak.

Huo Lihui, chief statistician at the NBS service industry survey centre, attributed the factory slowdown mainly to seasonal factors. These included a pullback in overseas orders after a surge the previous month, softer consumer demand after the holiday period and a seasonal slowdown in basic raw materials. The bureau also pointed to demand pulled forward ahead of the early October National Day holiday and to uncertainty in the international environment.

Price pressures eased but remained elevated. The raw material purchase price sub-index fell 4 points to 56.8 and the output price gauge fell 2.3 points to 51.7. Both remained above their levels a year earlier, a sign that industrial prices are still relatively firm.

The data suggest the economy lost momentum at the start of the fourth quarter after a modest recovery in the third, as Beijing works to keep annual growth within its 4.5% to 5% target. Policymakers have signalled they are prepared to add stimulus if conditions deteriorate, and October’s figures are likely to sharpen market focus on whether further support arrives before year-end.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran says two tankers hit mines in Hormuz as Tehran offers two-day reopening plan
item.description:
A claim that mines are now disabling tankers in Hormuz, including a supertanker, raises the perceived physical risk of every transit, not just those Iran targets, and is likely to feed through to freight rates, war-risk insurance premiums and the geopolitical premium in crude. The reopening plan offers a theoretical path to restored flows, but its conditions reach well beyond shipping, so traders are likely to treat it as a negotiating position rather than a near-term supply fix. Until there is independent confirmation of the incident and a US response to the proposal, upside risk to oil looks more immediate than the prospect of relief.

-

Iran is using both mines and mediation in Hormuz, claiming two tankers were blown up on an unapproved route while offering to reopen the strait in two days, if Washington meets a demanding price.

Summary:

  • Iran’s IRGC navy said two oil tankers, one of them a supertanker, struck mines and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday evening local time, according to Iranian state media
  • The IRGC said the vessels had switched off navigation systems and were attempting a covert, unauthorised transit with US military support; this claim has not been independently verified
  • Iran has restricted passage through the strait and attacked ships it says break those rules, seeking to assert control of the waterway and pressure the US
  • After mediation talks in Qatar and Pakistan, Iran’s foreign minister set out a two-day plan: US compliance measures on day one, reopening of Hormuz and restored shipping on day two
  • Iran’s conditions include new navigation routes through the strait, unfrozen assets, an end to regional conflicts including Lebanon, lifting of maritime blockades, exemptions for Iranian oil exports and removal of sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said two oil tankers, including a supertanker, struck mines and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday evening local time, alleging the ships had been travelling along a route Tehran had not authorised. The claim, carried by Iranian state media, came as Iran’s foreign minister outlined a two-day plan that he said could reopen the waterway and restart negotiations with Washington.

According to the IRGC, the two vessels had turned off their navigation systems and were attempting a covert passage with US military backing before the mine strikes forced them to stop. The initial reports did not name the tankers or give their flags, cargoes or the condition of their crews, and the IRGC’s account of US involvement has not been independently confirmed.

The incident fits a broader pattern in the strait. Iran has imposed restrictions on vessels seeking to pass through Hormuz and has attacked ships it says breach those rules, as it seeks to assert control over one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints and increase pressure on the United States.

On the diplomatic track, Iran’s foreign minister said that following mediation talks in Qatar and Pakistan, Tehran had agreed to a sequenced proposal. Under the plan, the US would carry out a package of compliance measures on the first day, and the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened and shipping restored on the second. He said any resumption of Iran-US negotiations would depend on Washington fulfilling its commitments.

Iran set out those commitments as agreement on new navigation routes through the strait, the unfreezing of Iranian assets, an end to regional conflicts including in Lebanon, the lifting of maritime blockades, exemptions for Iranian oil exports and the removal of US sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum.

Taken together, the two developments send mixed signals. The plan offers a defined route to restored shipping, but the list of conditions extends far beyond navigation into sanctions, frozen funds and wider regional conflicts, which suggests a quick US acceptance would be difficult. The demand for new navigation routes would also effectively formalise the kind of Iranian-approved passage the IRGC says the two tankers avoided. Markets will now be watching for independent confirmation of the mine strikes, details of the vessels involved, and any response from Washington to Tehran’s proposal.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: What protects Japan’s economy? And what does it mean for the yen?
item.description:
What protects Japan’s economy? And what does it mean for the yen?

Japan has global businesses, valuable overseas investments and a central bank moving away from years of very low interest rates. But a strong economy does not automatically mean a strong currency.

Look at a Japanese castle surrounded by a moat and a simple idea comes to mind: the water and walls help protect what is inside.

An economy can have defenses too. Japan’s include businesses that sell products around the world and substantial investments in other countries. But its defenses have gaps, including a reliance on imported energy.

That raises an interesting question for anyone watching the Japanese yen: if Japan has so many economic strengths, why can its currency still struggle against the US dollar?

The answer begins with a distinction. The strength of an economy and the price of its currency are connected, but they do not always move together.

Japan’s economic moat

Japan is home to companies known around the world for cars, machinery, electronics and other products. It also supplies materials and equipment used to make computer chips.

When people and businesses abroad buy Japanese products, that creates income for Japanese companies and supports jobs at home. Japan’s exports of cars, semiconductors and chipmaking equipment grew in September, according to trade figures reported by The Japan Times.

Japan also owns substantial investments overseas. Think of these as assets held in other countries by Japanese businesses, investors and institutions. Taken together, Japan’s overseas assets exceeded what it owed to the rest of the world at the end of 2025, according to Japan’s Ministry of Finance.

These are useful strengths. But the moat is a metaphor, not a shield that guarantees Japan will avoid economic trouble or that the yen will gain value.

Where the moat has a gap

Japan relies heavily on other countries for oil and natural gas. Its government says the country produced the equivalent of just 16.4% of its energy needs domestically in the 2024 financial year. enecho.meti.go.jp

That matters because many energy purchases are priced in US dollars.

Imagine a Japanese company needs $100 to buy fuel. If one dollar costs 150 yen, it needs 15,000 yen. If the dollar rises to 160 yen, the same $100 costs 16,000 yen.

The fuel’s price in dollars did not change. But the company needs more yen to pay for it.

This is one reason a weaker yen can add to costs in Japan. It can also affect households when businesses pass some of their higher costs on to customers.

A weaker yen can help some exporters, though. If a Japanese company earns dollars overseas, those dollars can be worth more yen when converted back. The actual effect on a business depends on where it makes its products, what it imports and its other costs.

The takeaway: a weaker currency can help some parts of an economy while hurting others.

Why Japan’s interest rates matter for the yen

Another part of the story is the cost of borrowing money.

For many years, Japan kept interest rates very low. That made it relatively cheap for some investors to borrow yen and use the money to buy assets elsewhere that offered the possibility of higher returns.

If borrowing yen becomes more expensive, that strategy can become less appealing. Investors must also consider the risk that exchange rates move against them. If the yen strengthens while they owe yen, paying back what they borrowed can become more expensive in their own currency.

On October 30, the Bank of Japan kept its main interest rate at 1.25%. The central bank also left the door open to raising rates later as it watches price pressures. One of its nine decision-makers wanted a rate increase at the meeting. www.reuters.com

Why does the bank care about prices? Inflation means that, overall, the prices people pay for goods and services are rising. Japan’s central bank spent years trying to move away from a period when prices were often barely rising or falling. Now it is also watching the risk that inflation could rise too much.

Higher interest rates can help slow price increases by making borrowing more expensive. But they can also make life harder for borrowers and businesses, so central banks must weigh both sides.

The dollar is on the other side of the moat

Even if Japan raises rates, that does not guarantee that the yen will strengthen against the dollar.

The reason is simple: an exchange rate compares two currencies.

USD/JPY tells us how many yen it takes to buy one US dollar. If the number rises, the dollar is strengthening against the yen. If it falls, the yen is strengthening against the dollar.

Investors therefore pay attention to what is happening in both Japan and the United States. For example, if Japanese interest rates rise but US rates are also expected to rise, the dollar may remain attractive to investors.

And markets often move based on what investors expect to happen. If traders already expect Japan to raise rates, the decision itself may not produce the reaction some readers anticipate.

What to watch next

Japan’s economic moat has real strengths, but those strengths do not tell us exactly where the yen will trade next.

For now, a useful question is whether investors expect Japan’s interest rates to rise further, and how those expectations compare with what they expect in the United States. Energy costs and the effect of a weaker yen on prices in Japan are also worth watching.

The other part of the picture is the market itself: how will USD/JPY behave as investors weigh those developments? The economic story provides context. The price chart can help us examine how the dollar and yen are responding.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin got spooked this Halloween. Is a monster rebound brewing or another crypto nightmare?
item.description:
Risk-off sentiment was kinda scary across asset classes heading into Halloween 2026, driven by heavy tech distribution, crypto security shocks, and cross-market margin calls.

As Greg at investingLive.com detailed, the Nasdaq suffered its worst monthly drop since March 2025 as mega-cap tech and semiconductor names tumbled, creating a stark divergence between growth shares and the broader market.

That selling pressure quickly spilled over into digital assets, with Greg highlighting that Bitcoin tested critical technical support as Binance security fears triggered defensive de-risking.

The fallout hit alternative tokens even harder, with Giuseppe Dellamotta at investingLive.com noting that Ethereum broke below minor support levels following the Binance exploit, precipitating a cascading wave of liquidations across leveraged positions.

Even traditional safe havens were not immune to liquidity needs; according to Giuseppe's latest analysis, gold absorbed forced liquidations to cover equity and crypto margin calls, even as underlying macro tailwinds and falling real yields leave the fundamental backdrop intact.

Bitcoin's Halloween trick or treat: Can BTC rebound after a $6.3 billion crypto scare?

Bitcoin is showing early signs of recovery after falling toward $76,300, but the Binance security breach, Nasdaq's AI-spending selloff and resistance near $79,000 leave traders with an uncomfortable question: Is the worst over, or is another scare coming?

Bitcoin is trying to recover from its sharp October selloff, but the technical evidence does not yet confirm a bullish reversal. After falling from nearly $84,800 to $76,300, BTC/USD has begun stabilizing. The question this Halloween is whether buyers can reclaim $79,000, or whether the recent lows are about to be tested again.

Bitcoin has plenty of reasons to feel spooked this Halloween

It has been a frightening end to October for risk assets, and Bitcoin has not escaped the selling.

On October 30, the Nasdaq Composite fell approximately 2.9%, as investors questioned the enormous amounts of money technology companies are investing in artificial intelligence.

Reuters reported that the Nasdaq 100 was facing more than $2 trillion in market-value losses for October, with AI infrastructure spending and concerns about future returns weighing on investor sentiment.

But Bitcoin had another monster lurking in the shadows.

On October 29, cryptocurrency exchange Binance suffered a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets. This Halloween, the real fright didn't come from ghosts or goblins, but from crypto thieves who left behind a multibillion-dollar nightmare!

In its October 30 security update, Binance said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to address the losses, while approximately $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen. The exchange also temporarily suspended withdrawals while conducting security checks.

That response may help restore confidence, but the investigation remains ongoing.

These developments created two distinct sources of uncertainty: pressure on risk appetite across financial markets, and a serious security shock within the cryptocurrency industry itself.

Neither explains every dollar of Bitcoin's decline. In fact, the technical deterioration had already been developing before the latest headlines.

The Bitcoin chart was already showing weakness

Bitcoin's broader price structure has been deteriorating for several weeks.

The cryptocurrency traded around $87,378 on September 21, approximately $87,175 on October 2, and then formed another significant high near $84,782 on October 21.

Those declining highs were an early warning that buyers were struggling to regain control.

The subsequent break below support around $78,507 added to the bearish picture.

By October 30, Bitcoin had fallen to approximately $76,300, representing a decline of about 10% from its October 21 high.

That decline matters, but something else in the market data deserves attention.

Where Bitcoin traders are doing business has shifted lower

One particularly interesting development is the downward movement in Bitcoin's daily point of control, or POC.

The POC identifies the price at which the greatest trading volume occurred during a specified period. It helps show where market participants have been most active.

In the analyzed BTC/USD market, that level shifted considerably:

  • October 21: Approximately $84,600

  • October 28: Approximately $81,400

  • October 29: Approximately $79,000

  • October 30: Approximately $77,000

Notice what happened around October 28.

Bitcoin briefly improved its trading structure, with meaningful activity returning toward $81,400. But that recovery failed, and the most active trading price subsequently shifted much lower.

This is an important distinction.

Bitcoin can bounce in price without demonstrating that buyers are willing to maintain positions at higher prices.

A more convincing recovery would involve not only higher prices, but also sustained trading activity at those higher levels.

There is a qualification here: these volume-profile observations come from a limited BTC/USD market sample, not consolidated trading across all Bitcoin exchanges. They provide useful context, but do not establish market-wide institutional buying or selling.

Could Bitcoin's next move be a Halloween treat?

There are early indications that the selling pressure may be changing.

October 29 was particularly weak, with a daily trading range of approximately $4,000 and a close near the session lows.

October 30 was different.

Although Bitcoin extended its decline toward $76,300, buyers subsequently pushed the price back above $77,000.

The four-hour chart also began developing higher lows following that decline, while shorter-term price action improved.

This is consistent with an emerging rebound.

However, the daily structure remains bearish, and the recovery has yet to overcome the resistance levels created during the preceding selloff.

In other words, the shorter-term chart is beginning to look more encouraging than the daily chart.

That disagreement is not unusual near possible turning points. It also creates a useful test for traders: will the improving short-term structure eventually strengthen the larger trend, or will the larger bearish trend overwhelm the rebound?

Bitcoin price levels: Where the next trick or treat may be decided

The following BTC/USD levels are based on the October 31 analysis snapshot, not a continuously updated trading quote.

The upside: What buyers need to reclaim

$77,800-$78,150: The first recovery test

This is the first important area where Bitcoin may encounter sellers. Reclaiming it would improve the immediate outlook, but would not be sufficient to establish a larger reversal.

$78,507-$78,643: Broken support becomes resistance

This area previously helped support Bitcoin. After the breakdown, it becomes an important place to watch for renewed selling.

A successful recovery through former support would be another constructive development.

$79,000-$79,050: The more important decision area

This is the level I would pay particular attention to.

The area around $79,000 represents an important structural test. In fact, investingLive's earlier Bitcoin technical analysis identified $79,146 as the lower boundary of the previous consolidation range before sellers took control.

A sustained recovery through this region, preferably followed by a successful retest, would strengthen the bullish argument.

It could shift attention toward approximately $80,500 and eventually the $81,400-$81,800 region.

The important word is sustained. Briefly trading above resistance is not the same as holding above it.

The downside: What would give sellers another opportunity?

$77,000-$77,150: Immediate support

This area is important for maintaining the developing rebound.

If Bitcoin begins losing this region and fails to recover it, the shorter-term improvement would become less convincing.

$76,300: The recent low and critical downside test

A decisive breakdown below $76,300, followed by continued trading beneath it, would strengthen the bearish continuation case.

That could bring the lower support region around $76,050-$74,935 into focus.

However, there is another possibility worth remembering.

If Bitcoin briefly breaks beneath $76,300 but quickly recovers above it, the apparent breakdown could prove false. That would be a very different signal from continued selling below the low.

For traders, the reaction to the level can matter more than the initial break.

Three scenarios for Bitcoin after Halloween

1. The treat: A recovery that becomes more convincing

Bitcoin maintains support around $77,000 and advances through its initial resistance levels.

A sustained move above $79,050 would improve the technical outlook, potentially allowing the recovery to extend toward $80,500 and the higher $81,400-$81,800 resistance region.

Buyers would still need to demonstrate that the market can hold those higher levels.

2. The trick: A rebound that attracts fresh selling

Bitcoin recovers toward $78,150-$79,050, but sellers return and prevent a sustained breakout.

A subsequent loss of $77,000 would increase the risk of another test of $76,300.

If that low fails decisively, the bearish trend would remain in control, with the next lower support region coming into focus.

3. The patience scenario: More consolidation before the next major move

Bitcoin could also spend additional time fluctuating between nearby support and resistance without providing a convincing directional signal.

That would not be particularly exciting, but it could help establish whether the recent selling pressure is genuinely fading.

With cryptocurrency markets continuing to trade over the weekend, traders should also be mindful of abrupt moves and potentially thinner liquidity.

What could change Bitcoin's outlook next?

Beyond the chart, the Binance incident deserves continued monitoring.

Further verified information about recovery of stolen funds, withdrawal services and the exchange's promised proof-of-reserves disclosures could influence confidence in cryptocurrency trading infrastructure.

Broader market sentiment also matters.

The recent Nasdaq decline reflected growing investor concerns about the cost and potential profitability of the AI investment boom. If technology stocks remain under pressure when US markets reopen, it could continue weighing on speculative assets, including Bitcoin.

Conversely, stabilizing equity markets and reassuring developments from Binance could create a more favorable environment for a Bitcoin recovery. Neither would guarantee a rally.

Ultimately, price action needs to confirm whether confidence is actually returning.

My Bitcoin takeaway this Halloween

Bitcoin has shown enough short-term improvement to make a rebound worth watching, but not enough to declare the bearish trend finished.

For me, the most meaningful levels are relatively straightforward:

$76,300 is the downside line that buyers need to defend. $79,050 is the upside level that would make a more substantial recovery increasingly credible.

Between those levels, patience may prove more valuable than trying to predict every short-term move.

And perhaps that is the lesson for traders this Halloween.

Bitcoin might have a treat waiting after a frightening October. But before reaching for the candy, I would like to see the market prove that the latest recovery is more than another trick.

Market analysis dated October 31, 2026. Bitcoin trades continuously, and the October 31 daily session was incomplete at the analysis cutoff. Price levels are technical reference areas, not guaranteed outcomes. Trade at your own risk.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 30 Oct: It’s a wrap: Nasdaq tumbles as AI costs worry investors; Fed speakers keep hikes in play
item.description:
• Nasdaq suffers worst month since March 2025 as technology stocks tumble
  • Bitcoin tests key support as Binance security fears weigh
  • Week ahead: Elections, rate decisions and jobs take center stage
  • Earnings next week: Can Apple, Palantir and AMD restore confidence?
  • Fed’s Logan: At least two more quarter-point rate hikes needed
  • Carney: Canada, EU working toward deepest possible partnership, short of accession
  • Fed’s Daly: AI matters for near- and medium-term policy
  • Fitch on UK Budget: Policy continuity leaves a tough delivery challenge
  • Fed's Barkin: Direction of travel is straightforward for the Fed
  • Canada GDP for August 0.0% vs 0.2% estimate
  • US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected
  • Morning Kickstart: Tech hammered as Amazon and Intel tumble; oil rises despite peace talk
  • investingLive European session wrap: AI spending fears spook tech stocks; dollar falls alongside yields, gold

October ended with investors taking a harder look at the cost of the AI boom. Technology led a broad stock-market decline as disappointing reactions to Amazon and Intel earnings reinforced concerns about spending, profitability and cash flow. Strong demand remains part of the story, but investors are becoming more demanding about when that demand translates into returns.

The cross-market moves were revealing. Treasury yields declined even as several Fed officials argued for further tightening. Oil moved higher, keeping inflation concerns alive, while gold failed to benefit from lower yields. Bonds attracted defensive demand, but the protection did not extend across every traditional haven.

Dollar finishes mixed after recovering earlier losses

The dollar was mixed in the supplied late-session snapshot. Its strongest performance was against the euro, with EURUSD down 0.13% at 1.1164. Its weakest performance was against sterling, with GBPUSD up 0.11% at 1.3390.

USDJPY slipped 0.06% to 157.59, while USDCHF rose 0.05% to 0.8246. USDCAD edged down 0.06% to 1.3979 despite disappointing Canadian growth data. AUDUSD gained 0.07% to 0.7032, while NZDUSD fell 0.07% to 0.5629.

The mixed finish marked a recovery from the dollar’s broader weakness earlier in the session. Falling U.S. yields provided a headwind, but the currency market did not deliver a uniform risk-off response.

Treasury yields fall despite calls for more tightening

Treasury yields were lower across the curve in the supplied snapshot. The 2-year yield fell 6.43 basis points to 4.5917%, the 5-year declined 7.87 basis points to 4.7233%, the 10-year dropped 5.86 basis points to 4.9303%, and the 30-year eased 1.76 basis points to 5.3114%.

The larger declines in shorter and intermediate maturities steepened the curve. The move was consistent with defensive demand as stocks weakened, even though the Fed commentary offered little reassurance that the tightening cycle was finished. Lower yields alone were insufficient to offset the concerns facing technology shares.

U.S. stocks: Nasdaq leads the retreat

The supplied end-of-day index readings showed:

  • Dow industrial average: −573.08 points, or −1.09%, at 51,775.17.

  • S&P 500: −140.32 points, or −1.82%, at 7,580.07.

  • Nasdaq Composite: −747.73 points, or −2.86%, at 25,437.00.

  • Russell 2000: −47.37 points, or −1.66%, at 2,811.84.

  • Nasdaq 100: −1,017.66 points, or −3.46%, at 28,384.85.

The selling extended beyond technology, but the Nasdaq indices carried the heaviest burden. The Dow held up better on a relative basis, although a decline of more than 570 points still reflected a difficult session.

AI faces questions about financing and returns

Amazon and Intel remained central to the earnings concerns. Investors questioned how much spending would be required to sustain AI growth and how quickly that investment would produce stronger profits and cash flow.

A separate Financial Times report covered by InvestingLive added a financing concern: Blackstone reportedly told Anthropic that it might not obtain an investment-grade credit rating after its IPO. This was a reported possibility, rather than a ratings decision, but it sharpened the focus on borrowing costs. Intel was down more than 30% in that afternoon report, with substantial losses across chip and infrastructure suppliers including AMD, Arm, Marvell, Astera Labs and Coherent. Those were intraday readings.

European stocks mostly lower

European markets also finished mostly lower, with the UK holding a modest gain:

  • Germany’s DAX: −221.47 points, or −0.85%, at 25,818.22.

  • France’s CAC 40: −0.58 points, or −0.01%, at 7,969.43.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: +7.73 points, or +0.07%, at 10,729.79.

  • Spain’s IBEX: −204.70 points, or −1.09%, at 18,652.90.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: −501.39 points, or −1.02%, at 49,290.91.

Fed speak: More tightening remains on the table

Today’s Fed commentary carried a predominantly hawkish message, although the speakers differed in how directly they addressed the next policy move. Barkin favored gradual adjustment, Musalem argued for another increase soon, and Logan outlined a minimum of two additional quarter-point hikes. Daly concentrated on AI’s implications for the Fed’s inflation and employment objectives.

Richmond Fed President Barkin described the direction of policy as straightforward, with the pace still open to debate. He favored a gradual approach but pointed to resilient consumer spending, broad business cost pressures and companies preparing to pass those costs to customers. His comments on AI were particularly relevant to the day’s market debate: the investment surge is adding demand and straining supply chains, creating inflation pressures that monetary policy can lean against. His assessment suggested that economic resilience continues to give the Fed room to address persistent inflation.

San Francisco Fed President Daly focused on how AI affects both price stability and employment. She emphasized that those effects matter for policy in the near and medium term. Her remarks did not establish a preference for a hike or a pause. The takeaway was that AI’s effects on the economy are already relevant to current monetary policy decisions.

St. Louis Fed President Musalem delivered a more explicit call for action, saying rates would need to rise again soon. He viewed monetary policy and overall financial conditions as accommodative, with inflation unlikely to ease sufficiently without additional Fed action. Higher bond yields had tightened conditions, but not enough in his assessment. His preference was to act earlier in smaller increments, reducing the risk that delayed action eventually requires a sharper adjustment. A strong economy and labor market supported that approach, while inflation risks remained tilted higher.

Dallas Fed President Logan was the most specific about the amount of tightening she considered necessary. She called for at least two more quarter-point increases to make policy modestly restrictive, followed by a pause to assess whether further action was needed. Skipping a meeting, in her view, would not change the destination. Gradual adjustments could help households, businesses and investors adapt, but she regarded the lack of progress toward the 2% inflation target as unacceptable. Her message made clear that a pause should not automatically be interpreted as the end of tightening.

For traders, the distinction matters: Treasury yields fell on the day, but these remarks did not amount to a dovish shift from the Fed.

Economic data: Labor costs moderate, growth signals soften

The U.S. Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9%. Wage growth eased to 0.7% from 0.9%, while benefit costs increased 0.9%, down from 1.0%. The report offered some reassurance on compensation pressures, although it did not resolve the broader inflation concerns raised by Fed officials.

Chicago PMI fell to 55.3, below the 56.1 estimate and down from 58.8. Activity remained above the 50 dividing line, but the pace of expansion slowed.

Canada’s August GDP was unchanged versus expectations for 0.2% growth. The advance estimate pointed to a 0.1% decline in September, reinforcing the picture of an economy struggling to build momentum.

German preliminary inflation also came in softer than expected. Annual CPI and harmonized inflation both slowed to 2.8%, below forecasts of 3.0% and 3.1%, respectively.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

WTI crude traded at $102.89, up $0.89 or 0.87% in the supplied snapshot.

InvestingLive’s oil coverage highlighted Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and reports of U.S. preparations for potential strikes on Iran. Those developments kept supply risks in focus heading into the weekend. Elevated energy prices also complicated the inflation outlook, even as Treasury yields declined.

Gold and silver join the selling

Spot gold fell approximately $146.24, or 3.64%, to $3,874.33. Silver dropped $3.0644, or 5.88%, to $49.0756. Copper also declined 1.75% to $6.4870.

Gold’s weakness stood out because Treasury yields were lower. That would normally provide support, but sellers retained control. InvestingLive’s gold analysis identified liquidation pressure associated with equity losses as a possible explanation: investors needing cash can sell liquid holdings such as gold to meet obligations elsewhere. That remains an interpretation of the selling, rather than a confirmed explanation for every transaction.

Silver’s larger percentage decline, alongside weaker copper, also left the more industrially sensitive metals under pressure.

Bitcoin remains under pressure

Bitcoin traded at $76,803, down $989 or 1.27% in the supplied snapshot.

The broader retreat from risk assets was compounded by concerns surrounding the reported Binance security breach. InvestingLive’s crypto coverage described exchange-security anxiety and leveraged liquidations as additional sources of pressure. Falling Treasury yields offered little relief as investors weighed both market-wide weakness and crypto-specific uncertainty.

Next week: U.S. elections, jobs and central-bank decisions

The November 2–6 calendar brings several important tests for markets, led by Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections and Friday’s employment report. The results will help shape expectations for government policy, economic growth and the Fed’s next move.

Monday starts with the U.S. ISM manufacturing report at 10:00 AM ET. Wednesday brings ADP employment at 8:15 AM ET and ISM services at 10:00 AM ET. Beyond the headline readings, traders will watch the employment and prices components for evidence of whether activity is slowing while inflation pressures persist.

Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes, spending, regulation and the administration’s legislative agenda. The September JOLTS report, due at 10:00 AM ET, provides another measure of labor demand ahead of payrolls.

Central banks also remain in focus. The Reserve Bank of Australia announces its decision Tuesday, November 3, Australian time—Monday evening in the U.S.—with several major banks expecting a 25-basis-point hike to 4.85%. The Bank of England follows Thursday with its rate decision and updated economic forecasts. Both events will test how policymakers balance inflation risks against the effects of tighter policy.

Thursday brings U.S. jobless claims and preliminary third-quarter productivity and labor costs at 8:30 AM ET. Friday is the main economic event: U.S. payrolls, unemployment and average hourly earnings at 8:30 AM ET, alongside Canada’s employment report. Preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment follows at 10:00 AM ET, with inflation expectations another important barometer. Together, the reports will help determine whether the economy remains resilient enough to support further Fed tightening.

What traders carry forward

The next session begins with three connected questions: can technology shares stabilize, can Middle East risks ease enough to take pressure off oil, and will incoming data justify the additional tightening several Fed officials favor? Friday showed that lower Treasury yields alone are not enough to restore confidence when earnings, financing costs and inflation remain in question.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
